description: A small hand-curated collection of 16 films and explicitly evidenced routes. Rankings are editorial, not personalized predictions or a complete film catalogue.

relationshipRules.direct_connection: A retrieved critic or scholar explicitly compares or groups these films on substantive grounds; this does not imply filmmaker-confirmed influence.
relationshipRules.curatorial_association: A publisher explicitly links the titles in its catalogue. The source's association is identified as curation, not scholarship or proof of influence.
relationshipRules.grounded_interpretation: CLOSEUP supplies the comparison. Each cited source supports one or both film-specific premises. Display the interpretation label.
relationshipRules.bidirectional: Pairs may be navigated either way. Reversing a route does not reverse historical influence.
relationshipRules.noPadding: Return only adjacent evidenced candidates for one or more trail films. Exclude every current trail film. Never fill empty results with unrelated catalogue items.
relationshipRules.noInferenceFromProgramme: Festival selection or awards alone do not establish an edge.

limitations: Korean aliases are practical search aliases, not a claim that every variant is an official Korean release title.
Source dates are null when no publication date was displayed. Festival dates denote the programme edition.

The Apple is consistently 1998 here; some catalogues use 1997. F for Fake appears as 1973, 1974 or 1975 across sources; this collection uses 1973, matching the supplied poster collection. Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One uses its 1968 production date; first screening was 1971.
Country and runtime metadata follow the cited catalogue's edition where available and may differ across releases; omitted runtimes are intentional.
All active evidence URLs were opened successfully for this catalogue. Sprio 2016 uses only the public abstract. Full text was retrieved for the 2009 Wide Screen paper.
Cannes's English The Apple route failed; the verified French official page is used with a translated summary. Unreliable NFB and Locarno routes are omitted from active evidence.
The catalogue is finite; trails can exhaust its evidenced neighbors. A source card describing only programme context must not be presented as a reason for a recommendation.
An edge's sourceIds describe that pair. A film's sourceIds include additional reading; do not display unrelated evidence as support for the selected edge.
Poster rights and production permission are outside this research file; posterAsset points to the existing supplied work assets.

sources.title: Filmic Performance – Authenticity and The Apple
sources.author: Margherita Sprio
sources.summary: Sprio pairs The Apple and Close-Up as works in which nonprofessionals restage lived experiences, raising questions about truth, performance and the director's power.
sources.locator: Abstract, PDF page 1; discussion of The Apple on pages 3–6.

sources.title: Performing History: Girlhood and Sib/The Apple (Samira Makhmalbaf, 1998)
sources.author: Margherita Sprio
sources.summary: The public abstract studies The Apple through reenactment, nonprofessional child actors, performance and girlhood.
sources.locator: Public Abstract section; chapter body is subscription content.

sources.title: The House that Mohsen Built: The Films of Samira Makhmalbaf and Marzieh Meshkini
sources.author: Adrian Danks
sources.summary: Danks connects The Apple with Close-Up and A Moment of Innocence through reenactment, and with Salaam Cinema through cinema's involvement in Iranian community life.
sources.locator: Later section on documentation and reenactment, followed by discussion of access to real participants.

sources.title: A Mirror Facing a Mirror
sources.author: Jared Rapfogel
sources.summary: Rapfogel examines self-reflexive storytelling in Close-Up and A Moment of Innocence, locating The Apple and The Mirror within a related Iranian fiction-documentary practice.
sources.locator: Opening discussion after the Close-Up synopsis; paragraphs on stories within stories.

sources.title: Don't Look at the Camera: Becoming a Woman in Jafar Panahi's Iran
sources.author: Jared Rapfogel
sources.summary: Rapfogel reads The Mirror as a response to The White Balloon: similar journeys through Tehran become a challenge to cinematic performance and adult authority.
sources.locator: Opening comparison of Panahi's first three features and subsequent The Mirror analysis.

sources.title: Iranian Cinema at MIFF 2000
sources.author: Ben Zipper
sources.summary: Zipper compares the restraint of Blackboards with The Apple and The Wind Will Carry Us, distinguishing Samira Makhmalbaf's moral tensions and settings.
sources.locator: Final five paragraphs on The Apple and Blackboards; final comparison with The Wind Will Carry Us.

sources.title: Close-up — film catalogue
sources.summary: The catalogue describes real participants playing themselves, and lists F for Fake and the Symbiopsychotaxiplasm collection among its related films.
sources.locator: Synopsis, Film Info and Related Films sections. The Symbiopsychotaxiplasm link is to a collection containing Take One and Take 2½.

sources.title: Certified Copy — film catalogue
sources.summary: The catalogue frames Certified Copy around authenticity in art and relationships; its related films include Close-Up and F for Fake.
sources.locator: Synopsis and Related Films sections.

sources.title: Through the Olive Trees — film catalogue
sources.summary: A film shoot and its actors' romantic lives overlap in the synopsis. The catalogue explicitly links Close-Up and Certified Copy as related films.
sources.locator: Synopsis, credits and Related Films sections.

sources.title: The Wind Will Carry Us — film catalogue
sources.summary: The synopsis follows a documentarian whose assignment is disrupted by village life. Close-Up is listed as a related film.
sources.locator: Synopsis and Related Films sections.

sources.title: F for Fake: all's well that ends with Welles...
sources.author: Geoff Andrew
sources.summary: Andrew discusses Welles's editing, authorship and playful uncertainty about documentary truth, describing a work that turns its inquiry toward its own maker.
sources.locator: Middle section on mixed footage, narrative construction and the essay-film form.

sources.title: Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Still No Answers
sources.author: Amy Taubin
sources.summary: Taubin examines Take One's repeated screen tests and crew conflict as questions about filmmaking, fiction, documentary and the director's authority.
sources.locator: Section beginning the analysis of Take One's theme-and-variation structure, before the separate Take 2½ discussion.

sources.title: Cameraperson: Getting Close
sources.author: Michael Almereyda
sources.summary: Almereyda explicitly compares Cameraperson with Sans Soleil as assembled documentary experiments, while distinguishing Johnson's exposed personal history and ethical encounters.
sources.locator: Comparison with Sans Soleil after the Vertov discussion; later passages on voyeurism and returning images to subjects.

sources.title: Cameraperson — film catalogue
sources.summary: The synopsis emphasizes filmmaker-subject relationships, camera intervention and a memoir assembled from documentary footage. Sans Soleil appears in Related Films.
sources.locator: Synopsis, Film Info and Related Films.

sources.title: Stories We Tell
sources.author: Tom Hall
sources.summary: Hall describes Polley's mixture of recreated scenes, interviews and home footage, showing how a family constructs memory and questions the telling of its own story.
sources.locator: Main review paragraphs on collective memory and the film's self-questioning. Page dated May 13, 2013; note states first publication September 7, 2012.

sources.title: Personal Effects: The Guarded Intimacy of Sans Soleil
sources.author: Jonathan Rosenbaum
sources.summary: Rosenbaum explicitly compares Sans Soleil and F for Fake as personal philosophical essays that use fiction, roaming perspectives and musical structures.
sources.locator: Final discussion comparing Sans Soleil with F for Fake; earlier analysis of fictional narrator and cameraman.

sources.title: The House Is Black — film catalogue
sources.summary: The synopsis describes Farrokhzad's pairing of poetry and direct observation, portraying everyday life in a leprosy settlement and affirming its residents' humanity.
sources.locator: Full public synopsis and director/year line.

sources.title: The Wind Will Carry Us: Dust to Dust
sources.author: Kaveh Akbar
sources.summary: Akbar studies the ethics of a filmmaker entering rural lives, and identifies the Farrokhzad poem recited in the film as the source of its title.
sources.locator: Passages on the documentarian's intrusion, the Koker Trilogy and Farrokhzad's poem.

sources.title: Salaam Cinema — IFFR 1996 programme
sources.summary: IFFR's substantive programme note describes casting sessions between documentary and fiction, with Makhmalbaf examining his own power over would-be performers.
sources.locator: Programme synopsis after film title, especially paragraphs on improvisation and the director's role.

sources.title: The White Balloon — MIFF 2006 programme
sources.summary: The programme describes a child's disrupted errand through Tehran and the near-documentary texture of Panahi's treatment of Kiarostami's screenplay.
sources.locator: Film-specific description below archive heading; final critical paragraph.

sources.title: La Pomme — Un Certain Regard 1998
sources.summary: The official French archive confirms Samira Makhmalbaf's debut in Un Certain Regard and identifies the Tehran family at the centre of the film.
sources.locator: French archive, title through cast. English route failed; the French page was opened and read. Summary translated.

sources.title: Takhte Siah — Official Competition 2000
sources.summary: The official archive records Blackboards in competition, its shared Jury Prize, and its story of teachers crossing Kurdish border regions.
sources.locator: Film-specific selection, synopsis and credits.

edges.why: Sprio and Danks explicitly connect these films through real people reenacting their experiences for a camera.
Danks links their blurred boundary between lived events and reenactment, while emphasizing The Apple's more immediate approach.
Rapfogel compares their nested stories: an event, its retelling, and the making of a film about that retelling.
Rapfogel locates The Mirror within the self-reflexive fiction-documentary practice exemplified by Close-Up.
Danks associates both with cinema's exceptional access to real people and its place in Iranian community life.
Danks names both while discussing cinema's power to involve everyday people in its own making.
Zipper directly compares their restraint toward characters facing urgent social pressures, despite different settings.
Zipper explicitly compares their directorial restraint, while distinguishing the moral tensions in Blackboards.
Rapfogel reads The Mirror as a response to The White Balloon, transforming a child's city journey through self-reflexive filmmaking.
Criterion explicitly lists F for Fake beside Close-Up. The pairing invites attention to performance, authorship and uncertain truth.
Criterion links Close-Up to the Symbiopsychotaxiplasm collection containing Take One; Taubin explains Take One's filmmaking-within-filmmaking.
Criterion explicitly connects the two titles, opening a route from performed identity to authenticity in art and relationships.
Criterion lists F for Fake as related to Certified Copy. Both source accounts make artistic authenticity central.
Criterion explicitly pairs them; the accompanying synopses describe lives that become entangled with film performance.
Criterion lists Certified Copy beside Through the Olive Trees, moving between performed relationships and their uncertain realities.
Criterion explicitly links these titles, connecting two different encounters between filmmakers and the lives they film.
Almereyda compares their assembled documentary fragments and reflective camerawork, while distinguishing Johnson's personal exposure.
Rosenbaum explicitly compares their philosophical essay forms, deceptive uses of fiction and musical arrangement of personal experience.
CLOSEUP interpretation: both accounts question what a camera's presence does to the people it observes.
CLOSEUP interpretation: move between two approaches to filming vulnerable people, attending to the observer's responsibility and the subject's humanity.
CLOSEUP interpretation: both remake recorded material into personal histories while exposing the choices involved in telling them.
CLOSEUP interpretation: both source accounts describe films that investigate truth while drawing attention to their own storytelling methods.
CLOSEUP interpretation: compare a family's reconstructed memory with a filmmaker and former policeman revisiting a shared past.
CLOSEUP interpretation: a route through children's experience of Tehran, connecting questions of girlhood with an everyday journey seen at a child's scale.
CLOSEUP interpretation: both readings bring girlhood into contact with performance, asking how a young person's experience enters a film.
CLOSEUP interpretation: auditions and screen tests expose the filmmaker's authority, letting production itself become the subject.
CLOSEUP interpretation: both turn a troubled film production into a means of inspecting the boundary between performance and life.
CLOSEUP interpretation: compare poetry joined to observed lives with an essay that reshapes documentary travel through a fictional voice.
CLOSEUP interpretation: both challenge a director's control by making the conditions and resistance of performance visible.
CLOSEUP interpretation: The Wind Will Carry Us quotes Forough Farrokhzad; The House Is Black offers her own filmmaking. This is a shared-poet route, not a claimed film influence.
CLOSEUP interpretation: both accounts put the filmmaker-subject relationship under scrutiny, from reenacted lives to a cinematographer's working encounters.
CLOSEUP interpretation: ordinary journeys expose wider social conditions, shifting from a child's city errand to teachers and young people crossing dangerous borders.
